title: Volume 4 · Scanning on the Floor: Barcode Capture and Mobile Counting
subtitle: Lessons 1–10: barcode data, scanning on documents, offline counting, recount discipline and what the floor actually needs
outcomes: Record barcode data so one item can carry several codes and units
Scan on Stock Entry and Stock Reconciliation without breaking valuation
Run a blind count with a handheld and reconcile it to the ledger
Design recount thresholds that catch errors without stalling the warehouse
Specify what a device must do offline, and how to prove nothing was posted twice

slides.title: Where the floor's time actually goes
bullets: Counting and keying are two different jobs, and keying is where the errors enter
A scan removes transcription, not judgement: somebody still decides what a discrepancy means
The measurable win is variance, not speed, because a clean count removes the stock write-offs that nobody budgets
Scanning pays for itself on the items with the highest movement, not on everything
Insist on a baseline before the project: count time, variance value and write-offs per month
slides.notes: Sell the project on variance, not on the romance of technology. A distributor that stops writing off stock every month has a number a finance director will defend. Take the baseline before anything is installed, because after the change nobody can reconstruct what counting used to cost.

slides.title: One item, many codes, one authority
bullets: ERPNext keeps barcodes as their own records, so an item can carry a supplier code and an internal code at once
A barcode can be tied to a unit of measure, which is how a carton scan becomes twelve units
Supplier codes change without warning, so the item record is the authority and the label is a convenience
Never let the same code point at two items; the scan will resolve to whichever record wins, silently
Print the internal code on the shelf label and keep the supplier code as an alias

rows: Open the item and add a barcode
Item Barcodes table gains a row
Add the supplier's own code as a second row
Set the unit of measure on the carton code
Scan of the carton asks for twelve
Search the barcode list for duplicates
Print a shelf label carrying the internal code
Record the mapping in the data pack
Supplier code to item, one row each

slides.notes: The duplicate check is the lesson that saves a client weeks. Two items sharing a code produces a count that is wrong in both directions and a report nobody can explain. Make the alias list an explicit deliverable, because supplier codes are exactly the field that drifts.

slides.title: A scan is a quantity entry with a twist
bullets: Scanning does not create a new kind of transaction; it fills the same rows faster and more accurately
On a Stock Entry the scan resolves the item, and the batch or serial asks for the same discipline as typed entry
Carton and unit codes must convert before the quantity lands, or the ledger gains twelve times too much stock
Scan into a draft first, read the totals, then submit, because a submitted movement needs a reversal
Teach the negative test once: scan the wrong code and watch the error, so nobody invents a workaround

rows: Open a Material Transfer to the floor
Scan the shelf label into the item field
Scan a code that belongs to no item

slides.notes: The last step matters more than the first five. When a scan fails, warehouse staff improvise, and improvisation is how a carton gets entered as one unit. Demonstrate the refusal while the trainer is still in the building, then write the exception path on the wall next to the scanner.

slides.title: Blind counts and the sheet that proves them
bullets: A blind count hides the expected quantity, which is the only way to find out whether the count is honest
The device holds the count locally and syncs once, so a dead spot in the warehouse does not stop the aisle
Every scan carries a timestamp, a user and a location, which is what makes the count auditable afterwards
Two people on the same shelf produce two counts; the reconciliation decides, not the loudest voice
The count sheet is a draft until somebody with authority posts the difference

rows: Create a Stock Reconciliation for the warehouse
Hand the aisle to the counter with expected quantity hidden
Scan each shelf label and key the physical quantity
Sync the device at the end of the aisle
Leave the difference unposted until reviewed

slides.notes: Blind counting is a cultural decision as much as a configuration one, and it is worth the argument. A counter who can see the expected number will produce it. Say this to the warehouse manager in front of the finance lead, because it is finance who carries the cost of a fabricated count.

slides.title: What the difference does to the books
bullets: Posting a count difference writes a stock ledger row and a matching accounting adjustment, never a deletion
The valuation of the difference uses the item's costing method, which is why a count on FIFO items needs care
A large negative difference is either theft, misplacement or a process error, and each has a different owner
Check the difference in value, not just in quantity, because a four-unit gap on a cheap item is not the same as on a van part
Attach the signed count sheet to the reconciliation so the number has a witness

rows: Quantity agrees with the count sheet
Stock Adjustment against the expense account

slides.notes: A reconciliation without its sheet is a number with no story. Insist on the attachment, because six months later the only question anyone asks about a write-off is who counted it and when.

slides.title: Scanning where the identifier is the stock
bullets: For a serialised item the scan is the record: scanning the same serial twice is a duplicate, not a second unit
Batch scanning needs the expiry read back, because the wrong batch is a compliance problem, not a clerical one
Turn on the setting that lets serial and batch fields be typed or scanned on stock documents, and teach it as the default
Scanning a serial that is not in stock must fail loudly rather than create it
For a distributor of regulated goods, the scan trail is the recall trail

rows: Confirm serial and batch entry is enabled for stock documents
Create a delivery for a serialised item
Scan a batch and read the expiry back
Attempt a serial that is not in stock

slides.notes: The refusal cases are the whole value of serialisation. A system that quietly accepts a serial it has never received gives a client false confidence in a recall. Walk the floor manager through both refusals, then write them into the SOP as expected behaviour rather than errors.

slides.title: The label is part of the system
bullets: A shelf label that will not scan is a stock error waiting for a busy week
Label stock, print density and laminate all change whether a scan works at arm's length in poor light
Reprinting a label must be a normal, logged action rather than a reason to key the code by hand
Test with the actual device the floor will use, not a phone in a bright office
Record label sizes and the printer model in the handover pack, because reordering stock is a weekly task

rows: Label prints at the right size

slides.notes: Most scanning projects fail at the label, not the software. The technical configuration is easy; the durable part is knowing which label stock, which density and which printer, written down so a reorder does not become a project.

slides.title: Thresholds, recounts and who signs
bullets: Set a variance threshold in money, not in units, because a thousand washers matter less than one pump
Above the threshold, a second counter recounts before anything is posted
Below the threshold, the count posts automatically and the monthly report samples it
Name the person who may approve a large write-off, and the person who may not
Publish the monthly accuracy figure so the floor can see whether the discipline is working
slides.notes: Thresholds turn an all-or-nothing control into a workable one. If every difference needs a manager, the floor eventually stops reporting differences, which is worse than a small write-off. Pair the threshold with published accuracy so the shortcut is visible.

slides.title: Prove nothing was posted twice
bullets: A device that queues scans offline will eventually send the same batch twice, so the design must assume it
Give every count or transfer a client-generated reference that the server rejects when repeated
After a sync, reconcile the device total against the voucher total before submitting anything
Never let two people hold the same aisle at once, because merging two counts is guesswork
Show the user the queue: what is pending, what failed and what was already posted
slides.notes: This is the one technical-adjacent idea a functional consultant must still own, because the failure is a doubled stock movement that nobody notices until the ledger stops reconciling. Insist on the visible queue and the duplicate refusal as acceptance criteria for any device, ours or a vendor's.

slides.title: The floor kit list and the SOP
bullets: Hand over a kit list: device, charger, spare battery, label stock, printer, and who replaces each
The SOP has four pages at most: label a shelf, count an aisle, fix a refusal, escalate a variance
Train two people per shift, because one trained person is a single point of failure
Record the accuracy baseline and the target so the improvement is visible in three months
Leave the exception register: every refusal, why it happened and what was done

rows: Variance per cent, before and after

slides.notes: The kit list is what separates a pilot from a working system. Spare batteries and label stock run out on a Friday, and if nobody owns the reorder, the scanner goes back in the drawer and the paper list returns. Leave the register too, so the next person inherits the exceptions rather than rediscovering them.

lab.title: Lab · Scan, count and prove a shelf at Seri Murni
steps: Add the supplier code as a second barcode on SM-BL200 and set the carton code to twelve units
Search the barcode list for duplicates and record any collision in the exception register
Scan the shelf label and the carton into a draft Material Transfer and read both quantities
Scan a serial that is not in stock and record the exact refusal message
Run a blind count on one aisle with expected quantities hidden and sync at the end
Post the difference only after checking it against the signed sheet and the stock ledger row
Test one deliberate duplicate sync and confirm the second send is refused with the same reference
Write the four-page SOP, the kit list and the accuracy baseline into the handover pack
lab.done: A scanning pilot with a counted aisle, a posted and evidenced difference, a duplicate sync refused, and a four-page SOP the warehouse can run without the consultant present.

quiz.question: Why is a duplicate barcode the most dangerous configuration error in a scanning project?
options: It slows the scanner down
A scan of that code resolves to one item silently, so both items count wrong
It prevents label printing
It blocks stock reconciliation
quiz.why: Two items sharing a code means the scan resolves to whichever record wins, with no error. Quantity is then wrong in both directions and the report cannot explain why.

quiz.question: What makes a count auditable six months later?
options: The reconciliation voucher number
The signed count sheet, device export and the user and timestamp on each line
The valuation rate used
The approval of the warehouse manager only
quiz.why: The voucher proves a number was posted; the sheet, export and per-line identity prove who counted what, which is the question actually asked about a write-off.

quiz.question: Why does a blind count produce a more honest result?
options: It is faster than a visible count
A counter who can see the expected quantity tends to reproduce it
It removes the need for reconciliation
It hides the item's cost
quiz.why: Showing the expected figure converts a measurement into a confirmation. Hiding it is the only way to learn whether the shelf matches the ledger.

quiz.question: What should always be verified after a device syncs a count?
options: That the device battery is full
That the voucher total equals the device total before submitting anything
That the label printer is online
That the count used the internal code
quiz.why: The line count and quantity must match the device export exactly. A short sync produces a reconciliation that posts a difference nobody counted.

quiz.question: Why set the recount threshold in money rather than in units?
options: Because units are hard to count
Because a thousand cheap parts matter less than one expensive component
Because valuation changes daily
Because the ledger is in money
quiz.why: Value is what the write-off costs. A unit threshold puts the same weight on a washer and a pump, and burns management attention on the wrong line.

memory.spine: A scan is only evidence when the label, the count and the voucher agree, and the difference has a signature.

device.label: Scan, confirm, recount, sign
expansion: Scan to capture, but read the totals back before anything is submitted
Confirm the barcode is unique to one item and converts the carton correctly
Recount above the money threshold before a difference is posted
Sign the sheet, attach it to the reconciliation, and keep the device export
Prove the sync once by sending it twice, and confirm the duplicate is refused

cards.q: What is the measurable business case for scanning on the warehouse floor?
cards.a: Variance and write-off value, measured before and after. Speed is nice; a distributor that stops writing off stock has a number finance will defend.

cards.q: Why must the barcode list be checked for duplicates before go-live?
cards.a: A code pointing at two items resolves silently to one of them, so both count wrong and no error is raised at the scanner.

cards.q: What turns a count difference into an auditable event?
cards.a: The signed count sheet, the device export with user and timestamp, and the reconciliation voucher that carries both as attachments.

cards.q: What must be proved about a device that queues scans offline?
cards.a: That the voucher total equals the device total, and that a repeated sync with the same reference is refused rather than posted twice.

cards.q: How is a recount threshold best expressed?
cards.a: In money per line, with a second counter above it and a named approver, because value is what the write-off costs.

trap.what: The pilot scans beautifully in the meeting room, so go-live is declared and the SOP is never written.
trap.why: Label stock runs out, a batch refuses to scan and one trained person is on leave, so the floor reverts to paper. Hand over a kit list, a four-page SOP, two trained people per shift and an exception register.

narration: Scanning is the part of stock accuracy that a consultant is asked about most and prepares for least. Start with the barcode data, because one item can carry several codes, including the supplier's own, and a carton code that resolves to twelve units. Then check for duplicates, since two items sharing a code will count wrong in both directions without ever raising an error. Scanning on documents does not create a new kind of transaction: it fills the same rows, so read the totals back before submitting, and demonstrate a refusal rather than letting the floor invent a workaround. Counting is where the money is. Run a blind count so the counter cannot reproduce the expected figure, let the device queue offline, and prove after the sync that the voucher total matches the device total, and that a repeated send is refused. Set the recount threshold in money, name the approver, attach the signed sheet with the device export, and publish a monthly accuracy figure. Finish with the unglamorous part that decides whether any of it survives: label stock, a spare battery, two trained people per shift and a four-page SOP.
